description: Somos Boreal Labs. Juventud que Innova, Crea y Transforma Nicaragua!
summary: DATEX is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) web app that tells anyone whether the climate where they live is really changing, or whether it is just natural noise. Pick any place on Earth and a NASA POWER variable (17 monthly variables since 1981, from MERRA-2 and CERES) and DATEX returns an honest verdict: Confirmed change, Not yet significant, or No clear trend. Because climate data have “memory”, an ordinary trend line raises false alarms in up to 49% of cases; DATEX combines two independent tests and cuts them to 8.2% in our Monte Carlo simulation. When the answer is “not yet”, it says how many more years of data are needed. It also compares places, shows satellite imagery, relates climate to UN demographic and World Bank indicators after removing trends, and includes a 3D urban-growth scenario for Managua, with horizontal expansion and vertical growth, validated against 2020–2023 land-cover change (AUC 0.857). Built for students, teachers and journalists: no sign-up, no API keys, open source.
details:
What it does. DATEX answers three questions for any coordinate on Earth: what is changing, by how much per decade, and whether it is real or chance. It loads NASA POWER monthly series (1981–2025), removes seasonality, and applies two independent tests: a prewhitened Mann-Kendall test with the Theil–Sen slope, and an effective-sample-size regression. The verdict has three levels, and “Not yet” comes with the number of years still missing. A Monte Carlo benchmark shows that with strong climate memory an ordinary regression raises false alarms in 49% of cases, against 8.2% for DATEX.

Features. Radar of all variables for a place, comparison of two places, satellite imagery over time (Landsat/Sentinel-2), UN population projections against the recent linear pace, a climate–society view that removes trends before correlating, labeled linear scenarios, and a global map of 2,592 cells with false-discovery-rate control.

Urban growth in 3D. Under Satellite, a scenario for Managua models how the city may grow in 2023–2050: horizontally (new 100 m cells, chosen with a logistic model of 2017–2023 land-cover change) and vertically (more floors, from real GHSL building heights that grow with income, concentrated in the dense core). It is driven by UN urban population, income and climate signals, with explicit assumptions and sensitivity tables. It is a scenario, not a forecast.

Impact. Students, teachers, local technicians and journalists can check a climate claim for their own place without statistical training. It is free, bilingual, needs no sign-up or keys, and is open source (MIT).

Tools. React, TypeScript, Vite, Recharts, MapLibre GL; Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio) for the statistics engine and the urban model; precomputed static data, hosted on GitHub Pages.

What makes it different and what we considered. Instead of showing a trend line and declaring change, DATEX says when not to worry and how long to wait. We considered the 50×60 km grid-cell limit, reanalysis discontinuities (we flag step changes with the Pettitt test), multiple testing, sensitivity to the chosen period, and accessibility. Planned next: validation against independent series (ERA5, GPM, INETER stations)
